hook: The instrument maker whose steam engine powered the Industrial Revolution.

pages.x: James Watt was born in 1736 in Greenock, Scotland, the son of a shipwright. Often ill as a boy, he was taught mostly at home, and loved taking things apart. He learned to make scientific instruments in London, and in 1757 opened a workshop at the University of Glasgow.
A famous story says that as a boy he sat watching the steam lift the lid of his aunt's kettle, and dreamed of its power. It was told long after his death, and is probably made up, but it stuck.

Asked to repair a model of the old Newcomen steam engine, he saw that it wasted most of its coal heating the cylinder up again at every stroke. On a Sunday walk in 1765 the answer came: cool the steam in a separate chamber.
pages.fx: His engine used only about a quarter of the coal, which made steam power cheap enough to use almost anywhere.

pages.x: In 1775 he went into business with Matthew Boulton, a Birmingham factory owner, who told a visitor: "I sell here, sir, what all the world desires to have: power." Their engines pumped water out of the tin mines of Cornwall.
He added gears that turned the up and down push of the engine into turning motion, a linkage he was proudest of, and a spinning governor that kept the speed steady by itself.
pages.fx: Steam engines could now drive the machines of cotton mills and factories, and later railway locomotives and ships.

pages.x: To sell engines to people who used horses to work their mills, he measured how much work a horse could do, and rated his engines in "horsepower".
pages.fx: Car engines are still rated in horsepower, and the unit of power, the watt, is named after him: every light bulb carries his name.

pages.x: Tired of copying out his business letters by hand, in 1780 he invented a press that copied a letter written in special ink onto damp paper. Offices used his copying press for more than a century.
Watt's engine powered the Industrial Revolution, which changed how people live and work more than anything since the invention of farming.
pts: Made steam power cheap enough for factories
Gave us the horsepower; the watt is named after him
